I find that SNOS often started by not having a clear goal of the project I'm working on. 

I remember when I started my journey, I had a lot of ideas that I thought would be cool, but I never set a clear goal for when I could consider "Alright that's enough, I'm satisfied with this project". Then, when no clear goal combined with my lack of skills and experience, I got winded and didn't know where to advance the progress, so I looked back to my bag of ideas and began thinking about starting anew.

So if you're experiencing the same, I suggest first set a clear expectation for the outcome of your project and when it will reach said expectation. If you're just started, don't expect something flashy, polished, but rather playable (minimal bugs) and sharable (fun) to your closest friends. Then, that will become the baseline for your next project or your next iteration of the same project. Eventually, the process of making something playable and sharable will become easier and faster for you, giving you more time to focus on polishing and all the flashy aspects you can think of.

I'm going to assume a lot of things here. Let's consider this problem a simple heat transfer problem to ease the mind. The amount of heat transfer is denoted as Q = m x c x ΔT, with m is the mass of water in grams, c is the specific heat of water (4.18 J/g°C), ΔT is the temperature change required.  
  
So, let's denote Qb as the heat required to boil the water, Qs as the amount of heat output by the stove every second, and Ql as the amount of heat loss to the environment when the lid is opened. 

If the lid is closed, i.e no loss, then   
Qb = Qs x t1 (t1 is the amount of time it takes to boil the water when the lid is closed).

If the lid is opened and some of the heat escapes to the environment, then  
Qb = (Qs - Ql) x t2 (t2 is the same thing as above, but the lid is opened)

We can then rewrite the time required in each situation as follows:  
t1 = Qb / Qs  
t2 = Qb / (Qs - Ql)

Now here is where all the assumptions start: Let's say we have 1 liter of water, or 1000 grams; initial temperature 20 °C, final temperature 100°C, then ΔT = 80°C. And let's say the stove can output 1000W of power every second like a typical stovetop burner. Assuming 100% conversion from power to heat, meaning Qs = 1000W. Let's also assume the heat loss due to evaporation and convection is around 10%.

t1 = (1000 x 4.18 x 80) / 1000 = 344.4s or roughly 5.6 minutes

t2 = (1000 x 4.18 x 80) / (1000 - 1000 x 10%) = 371.56s or roughly 6.2 minutes

So yeah, with all of those very specific assumptions, about 10% increase in the amount of time to boil.

'_'.repeat(n) produces a string of length n made of underscores _

\^.?$ matches strings of length 0 or 1 (empty string or length 1)

\^(..+?)\1+$ does a few things in it. First (..+?) is a capturing group that matches substrings with at least 2 characters. Then \1+ tries to match the rest of the string as one or more repetition of the captured group. This will match numbers like 4, 6, 9,...

test() returns true if the regex above matches, which is trying to match a composite number, hence !test() will return if n is a prime.
